sentences.text: The head of Psarolepis was constructed from several thick dermal plates covered in deep pock-marks and large pores. These pock-marked head plates contained a layer of porcelain-like material known as cosmine.
It had a strangely humped snout with nostrils positioned above the eyes, which were located just above the upper jaw.
The premaxilla and dentary bones featured large inner teeth alongside an irregular array of tiny outer teeth.
Psarolepis possessed a unique feature called 'parasymphysical tooth whorls,' where teeth extended upward at the front of the lower jaw.
The fin spines found in Psarolepis are characteristic of primitive jawed fishes, absent in the most primitive sharks, but common in more derived forms.
Fossils of Psarolepis were primarily found in South China, specifically at the Yulongsi, Xishancun, and Xitun Formations located about 10 km northwest of Qujing, Yunnan.
Remains were collected in 1981 and 1984 by paleontologist Min Zhu and colleagues and dated to the Early Devonian and Late Silurian periods.

When first described in 1998, Psarolepis was classified as a sarcopterygian (lobe-finned fish) due to skull and jaw similarities to primitive lungfishes. However, in 2001, researchers Zhu and Schultze provided evidence suggesting Psarolepis was likely a basal bony fish.
Today, Psarolepis is classified within the class Osteichthyes.

Estimates for the time range of Psarolepis vary; one source records it as 418 to 397 million years ago, while another lists the range as 422.7 to 413.02 million years ago. Both estimates span the Pridoli to Lochkovian periods.
